metadata.title: Ep - 15, Mayur Vihar Ph 1 Street Food Walk l Suji Momo + Chaap hi Chaap + Aunty Vada Pav + Hot chips
metadata.description:
In this episode of Delhi Neighbourhood Eats, we arrived at Mayur Vihar Phase 1. Our host is a local—Shipra, a passionate baker who left her job to start her own small bakery business. She took us around her neighborhood to explore some of the everyday food spots that locals love. What followed was a trail filled with comfort food, unexpected finds, and inspiring stories of women vendors carving out their space in the street food scene.
We began our walk with a sugarcane juice stall to beat the heat. Ganne ka raas always gives you a sugar rush and is incredibly refreshing, but it's best enjoyed in moderation. Here, the juice was mixed with mint leaves and lemon, which gave it a zesty twist.
Our next stop was a stall named China Town, a busy van known for its Chinese delicacies. But what really caught our attention was the unexpected presence of rajma chawal on the menu. Curious about how it would taste coming from a Chinese food stall, we gave it a try—and we were pleasantly surprised. The rajma was creamy, spicy, garlicky, and the beans were perfectly soft. A solid, comforting plate of food.
Then we visited Chatka Momo, a stall that lives up to its name. They serve vegetarian momos that are maida-free, made primarily from sooji with a small amount of whole wheat flour. We tried their paneer and soya momos, along with their veg spring rolls. What stood out were the four condiments served with the momos—schezwan sauce, peanut butter, mayonnaise, and mint chutney. The paneer momos were juicy and flavorful, while the soya ones were a bit dry, but overall, it was a satisfying experience.
As we moved further, we came across a South Indian food stall run by Jayalakshmi, a woman from Tamil Nadu. At the time we stopped by, there were no customers. In conversation, she shared how business had been slow, with South Indian snacks not being as popular in this area. Despite the competition, she continued to serve food with warmth and a smile. We tried her paniyaram and dosa, both of which had a comforting, homely taste. To help draw more customers, we suggested she experiment with ingredients like butter and paneer. She is working hard to make ends meet, and vendors like her truly deserve our support.
Next, we visited another woman-led stall called Aunty Ji Ke Mashoor Vada Pav. Originally from Bihar, she started this cart with her son, who learned to make vada pav in Mumbai. The soft buns were generously stuffed with green chutney, ghati masala, and a crisp aalu fritter. The taste was surprisingly close to the Mumbai original—simple, spicy, and satisfying.
We then made a quick stop at South Indian Hot Chips, a snack store that specializes in freshly made chips with distinct South Indian flavors. With branches across the city, they prepare daily fresh batches that are packed and even exported. We sampled kela chips, aalu pudina chips, aalu ginger chips, kathal chips, and aalu lachha chips—each one crisp and full of flavor.
The real indulgence began at Mitra Di Chaap, a local favorite for chaap lovers. The variety here was immense. On the owner's recommendation, we tried their veg keema kaleji, shahi paneer, dal makhani, garlic naan, pyaaz roti, Amritsari chaap, garlic chaap, and soya Punjabi tikka. Each dish was well-spiced, rich, and deeply satisfying—a proper chaap feast to remember.
We ended our trail with a sweet treat from Kremella, where we tried their indulgent Lotus Biscoff and Nutella cheesecakes. Rich, creamy, and impossible to resist, they were the perfect end to our street food journey. Finally, we closed the meal with a refreshing paan.
